sections.title: Introduction
sections.html:
How can one number summarize the level of a small set of observations?

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • Calculate an arithmetic mean.
  • Explain why the count belongs in the denominator.

2.2 Before you begin

  • Use addition and division.

sections.title: Key definitions and concepts
sections.html:
• Observation: One recorded value.
  • Sample mean: The sum of the observations divided by their number.

sections.title: Calculate the mean
sections.html:
For a nonempty finite sample of \(n\) values, add every value and divide by the count:

\[\bar x=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i.\]

For \(1,2,3\), the sum is \(6\), the count is \(3\), and the mean is \(2\). The mean has the same units as the observations.

interactions.prompt_html:
5.1 Written practice

Consider the observations \(1,2,3\).

Solve the following:

  1. Calculate their sum and count.
  2. Find the mean and explain the denominator.
Show a hint

What does the denominator count? Label each observation before choosing an operation.
interactions.solution_html: The sum is \(6\), count \(3\), so the mean is \(6/3=2\).

interactions.prompt_html:
5.2 Check your reasoning

What is the mean of \(1,2,3\)?
feedback: That is the first observation, omitting the others. Sum all three values, then divide by their count.
Correct: the sum6 divided by count3 is2.
That is the largest observation, rather than the average.
That is the sum; divide it by the three observations.
